greeting: Good morning, Bay View. It's a clear 39 degrees at dawn, and a south wind pushes us to about 57 this afternoon. Today: a new owner for the corner of KK and Bay, a veto-free city budget, a cozy tea house in Joyce Skylight Court, and a scooter that went for a swim.

top.title: Developer Tim Olson's group buys the KK and Bay Street corner for $625,000
top.dek: The one-acre site at 300 E. Bay St. and 2020 S. KK has two aging buildings; no plans are public yet.
top.body:
A one-acre property at the north end of Bay View, where Bay Street meets Kinnickinnic Avenue, has a new owner. Bay Street Development LLC, a group led by multifamily developer and investor Tim Olson, bought the site at 300 E. Bay St. and 2020 S. Kinnickinnic Ave. from Chases' Crossings LLC for $625,000, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported Tuesday.

The parcel holds two older commercial buildings. No redevelopment plan has been filed, but Olson has been involved in other apartment projects in the neighborhood, according to the report, and Urban Milwaukee also covered the sale.

Any new building there would need city approvals, and the Bulletin will follow it when plans go public. On the Bay View Town Hall Facebook group, neighbors were already trading ideas Tuesday, from apartments to senior housing.
top.source_name: In Business Madison (citing the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel)

image.alt: A low white commercial building with blue awnings on the Bay View site at Bay Street and Kinnickinnic Avenue

top.title: Mayor signs the 2027 budget with no vetoes, so the council's changes take effect
top.dek: It's the first veto-free city budget since 2014, keeping the council's road, library and pay changes in place.
top.body:
Update: Johnson let Tuesday's deadline pass without a single veto and signed the spending plan as amended. Urban Milwaukee notes no city spending plan has escaped vetoes since the one adopted in late 2014, and last year aldermen unanimously overrode all seven of his.

His statement called it good fiscal news, pointing to agreement on paving and public safety, while saying he still has concerns he'll work through in coming months. One likely flashpoint: the council's raise structure for city workers, which will probably need a later salary ordinance vote and gives him another chance to object.

Ald. Marina Dimitrijevic, who chairs Finance & Personnel, thanked him and called the signature a sign of "unity and alignment."

image.alt: Mayor Cavalier Johnson at the lectern in the Common Council chamber presenting his 2027 budget in September

development.title: City proposes zoning changes to allow more housing; comments are open through Dec. 11
development.dek: Cottage courts, more townhouses and smaller lots are in the draft; a drop-in session is Friday downtown.
development.body:
Milwaukee's Department of City Development released a package of proposed zoning code changes Monday meant to carry out the city's Housing Element plan. In neighborhoods like Bay View, the drafts would allow smaller lots and homes, cottage courts of three to 12 small houses around a shared yard (with zoning board approval), more townhouses, and flag lots that could let a home be built behind an existing house on a deep lot, Urban Milwaukee reported.

The proposals would also drop the formula that caps how many apartments fit on a property, letting the building's allowed size set the limit, and add design and setback rules for larger buildings next to single-family homes. They would not change any property's zoning district, and they would not broadly allow duplexes or triplexes in single-family areas.

Nothing is final: the drafts still need review and Common Council approval. The city is taking comments online through Dec. 11, and holds a drop-in session with no presentation Friday, Nov. 20, from 1 to 5:30 p.m. at the Zeidler Municipal Building, 841 N. Broadway.

image.alt: Aerial view of rows of Bay View houses and trees

schools.title: MPS climbs to 'meets expectations' on new state report cards
schools.dek: The district rose from two stars; 67 MPS schools met or beat expectations, while 76 fell short.
schools.body:
Milwaukee Public Schools moved up from two stars, "meets few expectations," to "meets expectations" in the state report cards the Department of Public Instruction released Tuesday, WPR reported. Statewide, 95 percent of districts earned three, four or five stars.

Within MPS, 67 schools were rated as meeting, exceeding or significantly exceeding expectations, 40 as meeting few expectations and 36 as failing to meet them. Superintendent Brenda Cassellius said students are showing growth but much work remains, with a focus on the new elementary curriculum and a new high school literacy curriculum.

Each school's report card, including Bay View's MPS schools, can be looked up on DPI's report card site.

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Jasher's Organic Tea House
spotlight.dek: A living-room tea house tucked into Joyce Skylight Court, with chai made from scratch and a violin solo this Friday
spotlight.body:
Walk through Joyce Skylight Court at 2680 S. Kinnickinnic Ave. all the way to the back, and you'll find Jasher's Organic Tea House in Suite 4. It feels more like a living room than a cafe: couches, quiet music, a shelf of board games and, out back, a pet-friendly patio.

Married couple Jack and Rumi DeDecker opened it quietly in late November 2025 and named it for their young son. The two learned the ropes selling at local farmers markets before taking on a storefront, and they still spend plenty of evenings there as a family.

The menu has more than 20 teas, and everything on it is USDA certified organic. The couple also skip flavorings of any kind, natural or artificial. Look for herbal infusions like vanilla rooibos and turmeric ginger tonic, green and white teas, ceremonial matcha, yerba mate and pu'er tuo cha, a compressed Chinese tea that holds up to several steepings. The best seller is Rumi's masala chai, made fresh daily with black Assam tea, fresh ginger, whole spices and jaggery. Jack told Urban Milwaukee, "I would say it's a top seller." Any tea can be iced, the butterfly-pea Blue & Violet Tango changes color when you squeeze in lemon, and this fall there's organic apple cider from Peck & Bushel in Colgate, spiced if you like. Snacks include popcorn popped in coconut and olive oil and scones and cakes from Rise & Shine Bakery.

Jasher's threw a three-day grand opening in June 2026, with a loyalty card launch, a tea-tasting contest and live music. It also finished a two-phase restoration of its patio, and in July it took its masala chai and iced teas to the Incredible India Festival at the Summerfest grounds. Lately it has hosted a Saturday morning run club and a community kit-packing event.

This week brings something new. On Friday, Nov. 20, Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra violinist Paul Hauer plays a solo set from 7 to 7:45 p.m., followed by an acoustic worship set led by Jack until 8:30. There will be free samples of a new chocolate mint chai, a blend of organic pu'er, cocoa shells, cinnamon, peppermint, vanilla bean and licorice root.

Jasher's Organic Tea House, 2680 S. Kinnickinnic Ave., Suite 4 (inside Joyce Skylight Court). Open Tuesday-Friday 4-9 p.m. and Saturday 9 a.m.-5 p.m.; closed Sunday and Monday. jashersorganic.com, @jashersorganicteahouse on Instagram.

history.title: Puddler's Hall, the iron workers' union hall that became a tavern
history.text: In the early 1870s, Bay View's iron puddlers built a union hall on St. Clair Street. More than 150 years later, Puddler's Hall is still pouring.
history.body:
The dark green building with maroon trim at 2461 S. St. Clair St. started out as a union hall. Iron workers at the Milwaukee Iron Company's rolling mill, the puddlers and boilers who worked molten iron into bars and rails, put it up in the early 1870s. Urban Milwaukee dates it to 1872, while Milwaukee Record says 1873. The workers used it for meetings, concerts and celebrations.

Those were the years when Bay View was a mill town. In May 1886, thousands of Milwaukee workers struck for an eight-hour day, and the march on the Bay View mill ended on May 5 when the National Guard opened fire, killing seven people. It remains the bloodiest event in Wisconsin's labor history. Today three signs above the tavern's front windows repeat the movement's slogan: eight hours for work, eight hours for sleep, eight hours for what you will.

In the early 1890s the union sold the hall to the Falk, Jung and Borchert brewery, and it became a tied house selling one brewer's beer. When that brewery was absorbed by Pabst, it became a Pabst tavern. Around the start of Prohibition it passed to the Barbieri family, who added a dance hall in back. Barbieri's Dance Hall ran until 1979. Milwaukee Record notes it was rumored to have been a speakeasy.

After that came a string of names, including Mardee's Party and Sue's Bay View Bandwagon. In 2002 a new owner renamed it Puddler's Hall to honor the building's roots and hung photos of the mill and early Bay View. Casey Foltz, a Bay View neighbor, reopened it in 2011 after a short closure. Milwaukee Record counts it as the city's second-oldest tavern, behind only the Landmark Inn near the airport.

It is still a neighborhood gathering place. The Bay View Table Tennis Club plays there on Thursdays, and the Milwaukee Guitar Club meets there too.
history.source_name: Urban Milwaukee, "Taverns: The 141-Year-History of Puddler's Hall," March 31, 2013
